A struggle is a hard, sustained effort against something that resists you or works against you. It is not just "difficulty" — it is active opposition over time. You are not passively suffering; you are trying, pushing, fighting. But the thing you are up against pushes back.

Think of it this way: if you are trying to open a door that is slightly stiff, that is not a struggle. But if you are pushing against a locked door with all your weight, repeatedly, desperate to get through — that feels more like one.

1. A hard, ongoing effort to deal with something difficult

This is the most common meaning. A struggle is the experience of fighting hard against a problem, obstacle, or painful situation — especially one that lasts a long time and drains your energy.

"Her struggle with depression lasted many years."
"For many families, the struggle to pay their bills never ends."
"Learning to read was a real struggle for him as a child."

Notice that in all three sentences, there is hardship, sustained effort, and an opponent — depression, poverty, illiteracy. You are not just having a bad moment; you are locked in a prolonged contest with something that does not give way easily.

2. A physical fight between two people or groups

When two people wrestle or physically fight each other — especially in close, intense contact — it can be called a struggle. This use often appears in crime, legal, or news contexts.

"There was a struggle between the two men before the police arrived."
"The gun went off during the struggle."

Here the word captures the idea of two forces colliding against each other — messy, close, and uncertain in outcome.

3. A long conflict or campaign, often political or social

Groups of people fighting collectively for rights, freedom, or justice over a long period of time are said to be engaged in a struggle. This meaning carries a sense of moral weight and historical importance.

"The struggle for women's right to vote lasted decades."
"Mandela devoted his life to the struggle against apartheid."
"The civil rights struggle changed the course of American history."
The Four Essential Qualities of a "Struggle"

Understanding these four qualities will sharpen your understanding of this word more than any definition alone.

Resistance. A struggle always involves something pushing back. You are not just doing something hard in isolation — there is an opposing force. It could be a disease, a system, poverty, another person, or even your own mind. Without resistance, it is simply hard work, not a struggle.

Duration. A struggle is not a single moment of difficulty. It unfolds over time — days, months, years, or even a lifetime. This is why we say someone struggled with an addiction or for freedom — these are long journeys, not brief incidents.

Effort. A struggle demands active exertion. You are trying. You have not given up. The very word implies that someone is putting in effort against the odds.

Uncertainty. In a true struggle, the outcome is not guaranteed. You might win or you might lose. This is what gives the word its emotional tension. If success were easy or certain, we would not call it a struggle.

The preposition you use with "struggle" changes the relationship between you and the difficulty.

Struggle with — you are dealing with something that is part of your life, often a condition or ongoing challenge.
"A struggle with anxiety." "A struggle with poverty."

Struggle against — you are opposing something, actively resisting it.
"A struggle against injustice." "A struggle against the disease."

Struggle for — you are trying to achieve or gain something.
"A struggle for survival." "A struggle for equality."

Struggle between — two forces, people, or sides are in conflict with each other.
"A struggle between two rival factions." "A struggle between duty and love."

An uphill struggle — a struggle in which you are always at a disadvantage, working harder than it seems fair to have to. The image is of climbing a hill — exhausting, relentless, slow.
"Convincing him to change his mind was an uphill struggle."

A power struggle — a conflict between two people or groups each trying to gain control or authority over the other.
"The company went into chaos because of a power struggle between the two founders."

An inner struggle / internal struggle — a conflict happening entirely inside a person's mind or heart, between two opposing feelings, values, or desires.
"He faced an inner struggle between telling the truth and protecting his friend."

A daily struggle — something that is difficult every single day, with no relief.
"For people living in poverty, finding enough food is a daily struggle."

This is where many learners make subtle mistakes.

A challenge can be exciting and motivating — it implies that success is possible and even rewarding. A struggle is heavier, more exhausting, and often painful. You welcome a challenge; you endure a struggle.

A battle is more intense and confrontational — it suggests two sides in direct, fierce combat. A struggle can be quieter, more internal, more grinding.

An effort simply means the energy you put into something. It carries no sense of resistance or hardship. A struggle, by contrast, always implies that something is working against you.

Hardship describes a condition — the state of suffering or difficulty. A struggle describes the response to that condition — the active fighting back. Hardship is what you face; a struggle is what you do about it.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

"Struggle" is not a neutral, clinical word. It carries real emotional weight. When someone says they are struggling or that something has been a struggle, they are telling you something honest and vulnerable — that they have been tested, that it has not been easy, and that they have had to fight. It deserves to be received with respect. This is why the word appears so often in the language of social justice, personal testimony, and literature — it captures both suffering and dignity at the same time.
